This pacing note is important because the course is now operating as a layered build, where concepts introduced today will be revisited and elaborated in subsequent lectures rather than exhausted immediately.

title: Valuation
section: Foundational Framing: From Holocene Stability to Anthropocene Risk
text:
Foundational Framing: From Holocene Stability to Anthropocene Risk

The Holocene as a Narrow Stability Regime
The lecture returns to the opening framing of the semester: human civilization and agricultural systems developed under the relatively stable climatic regime of the Holocene. This historical stability is characterized as a “Goldilocks” condition, not in the sense of perfection, but in the sense of bounded variability that supported predictable social and economic organization.


The Anthropocene as a Governance Challenge
The transition toward the Anthropocene is presented as a shift into a period where climatic and Earth-system stability can no longer be assumed. The concern is not simply environmental degradation in the abstract, but the loss of confidence in system stability that underwrote modern economic and social structures. The instructor emphasizes that human economic scale has become large enough to function as a dominant force in planetary systems.


Planetary Boundaries and the Donut Expansion
The lecture recounts an important conceptual shift made earlier in the course. Planetary boundaries remain central as metrics of ecological risk, but boundary thinking alone is insufficient. The framing therefore expands to donut economics, where ecological ceilings are evaluated alongside social foundations. This move prevents a one-sided environmentalism that ignores whether people remain above essential thresholds such as food, water, and energy access.

title: Valuation
text:
Reframing the Earth-Economy Relationship

From Separation to Embeddedness
A central conceptual correction in the lecture is the rejection of the old two-box framing in which Earth and economy are separate systems connected by a few arrows. Earlier economic thought often treated Earth primarily as a source of extractive inputs, and later added a reverse pathway for pollution and waste outputs. The instructor argues that this remains structurally inadequate.


Embedded Economy and Systemic Interdependence
The lecture insists that the economy is fully embedded within Earth systems and cannot be meaningfully modeled as external to them. In this view, there is no practical separation between economy and biosphere, only a dense web of interdependence. The challenge arises not because embeddedness is new, but because the scale of economic activity now pushes ecological thresholds.


Why Existing Navigation Is Inadequate
The instructor revisits an early-semester argument that society lacks an adequate navigational system for managing tightly coupled global problems. Prior course discussions established impacts and dependencies as linking concepts and connected them to the donut framework. However, those discussions remained mostly conceptual and did not yet provide an operational model capable of direct policy guidance.

title: Valuation
section: From Conceptual Framing to Analytical Tools
text:
From Conceptual Framing to Analytical Tools

Temporary Shift from Big Picture to Specific Methods
To build operational capacity, the course temporarily moved from systems-level framing to specific analytical tools. The circular flow diagram and interactive exercises were used as entry points for representing economic structure.


Limits of Static Circular Flow Representation
The lecture emphasizes that a standard circular flow diagram is a static snapshot. Because it lacks growth dynamics, it cannot directly represent how increasing economic scale changes pressure on ecological systems.


Growth Dynamics, Solow Logic, and Capital Accumulation
To address this limitation, the class extended the framework to include growth processes, especially capital accumulation and depreciation dynamics associated with growth models such as Solow. The instructor highlights capital deepening as a central mechanism: built capital enables additional production, and infrastructure increases productive efficiency.


Link to Policy Institutions and DSGE Practice
The instructor connects this theoretical structure to real-world policy modeling in central banks, where dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models are frequently used. Although mathematically more formal, these institutional models retain a familiar core structure involving utility-maximizing households, profit-maximizing firms, and policy levers such as interest rates and money supply.

title: Valuation
section: Why Earth-Economy Integration Is Newly Feasible
text:
Why Earth-Economy Integration Is Newly Feasible

A Threshold, Not an Incremental Improvement
The lecture advances the argument that contemporary Earth-economy integration represents a threshold shift rather than a minor technical upgrade. The aspiration to integrate these domains has existed for decades, but practical feasibility has changed.


Computational Capacity and Remote Sensing Resolution
The first enabling factor is computational scale. The second is major advancement in Earth observation data. Where coarse data once constrained modeling, contemporary workflows can use far finer spatial resolution, including ten-meter and sub-ten-meter products with frequent updates. This greatly increases both spatial specificity and temporal responsiveness.


Open-Source Scientific Infrastructure
A third enabling factor is the maturation of open-source scientific tooling. Platforms such as QGIS and InVEST allow researchers to execute technically serious workflows with transparent methods. The combination of faster computing, richer data, and open software ecosystem supports a new class of integrative models.

title: Valuation
section: Defining Earth Economy Modeling as a Research Program
text:
Defining Earth Economy Modeling as a Research Program

From Donut Framework to Navigational Instrument
The instructor describes donut economics as a valuable normative framework but insufficient on its own as a policy navigation instrument. Earth economy modeling is introduced as the effort to convert broad framing into detailed, operational systems that can guide decision-making within a safe and just corridor.


Core Definition and Required Components
Earth economy modeling is defined as the integration of general equilibrium macroeconomics with high-resolution Earth-system data under explicit two-way impact and dependency linkages, with sufficient empirical and structural detail to inform real policy choices. The emphasis on policy adequacy is critical, because highly simplified models may be elegant but cannot represent the heterogeneity required for practical governance.


Positioning in the 2025 Research Frontier
Drawing on a 2025 paper, the lecture presents Earth economy modeling as a frontier in sustainability science. The key claim is that the economy depends fundamentally on biospheric stability, while simultaneously acting as a driver of environmental change. Any model that fails to preserve this asymmetric dependency structure is expected to omit core system behavior.

title: Valuation
text:
GTAP-InVEST and the Publication Context

Model Integration in a PNAS Contribution
The lecture references GTAP-InVEST as a concrete implementation of Earth economy modeling published in PNAS. This serves as an existence proof that integrated architecture can be built and published at high scientific standards.


Visual Communication and Model Comprehensibility
The instructor includes a reflection on figure design in publication workflows, emphasizing that model communication is itself a substantive challenge. Different visual representations can significantly alter interpretability, and the process of translating technical structure into accessible figures is often contested.

title: Valuation
section: Literature Positioning and the “Has This Been Done” Challenge
text:
Literature Positioning and the “Has This Been Done” Challenge

The Central Credibility Question
A recurring challenge in proposing new modeling paradigms is the claim that the work is redundant because prior models already solved the problem. The lecture addresses this directly as a core scholarly burden.


AI-Assisted Systematic Review Strategy
To answer that challenge, the research team conducted a large-scale literature assessment using scripted, AI-assisted workflows to identify and evaluate candidate models. This substantially reduced the cost of systematic review relative to traditional manual approaches.


Comparative Mapping of 119 Models
The review assembled 119 models and positioned them along two dimensions: economic-sectoral detail and spatial-biophysical detail. Models varied from those with rich economic structure but weak Earth-system detail to those with strong biophysical representation but little or no explicit economy.


Frontier Interpretation and Research Direction
The resulting pattern resembled a production-possibilities frontier. The lecture’s argument is that future research must move outward on both dimensions simultaneously, because policy-quality Earth economy modeling requires high detail on both the economic and biophysical sides.

title: Valuation
section: Component One: Earth-System and Ecosystem-Service Representation
text:
Component One: Earth-System and Ecosystem-Service Representation

Six Ecosystem Services in the Integrated Framework
The first component of the architecture is explicit ecosystem-service modeling, including sediment retention, climate regulation, pollination, timber, coastal protection, and marine fisheries. These services are modeled through InVEST tools and associated global workflows.


From Watershed Models to Global Computation
A major technical milestone was scaling ecosystem-service computation from local or watershed contexts to global extent. Early global implementations handled fewer services and later work expanded coverage while maintaining computational tractability.


Computational Demands and Algorithmic Burden
The lecture notes that global modeling requires substantial computational engineering, including operations such as upslope and downslope flow-path calculations. The challenge is not merely conceptual integration but feasible execution at planetary scale.


Scenario Analysis and the Ghana Pollination Example
The framework supports comparison of alternative land-use trajectories under global scenarios. In the lecture example, a conservation-oriented pathway in Ghana preserved or improved pollination services relative to business as usual and was associated with substantial aggregate GDP gains when translated through economic pathways.


Broader Service Portfolio and Policy Comparisons
The same scenario-comparison logic is extended to carbon storage, fisheries, coastal protection, and water yield. The methodological point is that policy options are evaluated as explicit counterfactuals rather than as isolated indicators.


Coastal Protection and Habitat-Mediated Risk
Coastal modeling was described as especially complex because shoreline processes must be represented at segmented spatial units and linked to sea-level conditions, bathymetry, storm exposure, and habitat state. Natural barriers such as mangroves and coral reefs are modeled as protective assets that alter damage outcomes.


Water Yield and Nonlinear Economic Value
Water yield introduces a particularly difficult valuation problem. The same increase in precipitation can be beneficial or harmful depending on location and baseline conditions. Flood risk, reservoir recharge, irrigation constraints, and local scarcity all contribute to strongly nonlinear value relationships between hydrological outcomes and economic welfare.

title: Valuation
section: Interdisciplinary Bridging Through Natural Efficiency Curves
text:
Interdisciplinary Bridging Through Natural Efficiency Curves

Linking Biophysical and Economic Objectives
Before full model coupling, the lecture highlights a practical bridge known as the natural efficiency curve. This approach adapts production-possibilities logic so that one axis captures economic performance while the other captures ecological outcomes.


Willamette Valley Illustration and Win-Win Potential
Using earlier Natural Capital Project work in the Willamette Valley, the lecture describes how alternative land-use configurations can be compared against a baseline landscape. In some cases, alternative configurations improve both economic and ecological outcomes, demonstrating credible win-win moves.


Pareto Frontier Interpretation
When many feasible land-use configurations are evaluated, they define an efficiency frontier. Points on this frontier are Pareto-efficient, meaning improvement on one objective requires sacrifice on the other. This reframes planning as movement from interior inefficiency toward frontier efficiency, with explicit trade-off recognition.


Policy Relevance of Frontier Distance
The framework is policy-relevant because it can characterize where a country or region currently sits relative to feasible frontiers, how much improvement is available without hard trade-offs, and when true trade-off decisions become unavoidable.

title: Valuation
section: Interdisciplinarity as Institutional and Epistemic Challenge
text:
Interdisciplinarity as Institutional and Epistemic Challenge

The Tale of Two Disciplines
The lecture frames Earth economy modeling as a deliberate attempt to bridge a persistent disciplinary divide between economics and environmental sciences. Each domain contains internal specialization silos, but the cross-domain divide remains especially consequential.


Self-Referential Citation Patterns
A key indicator discussed is disciplinary self-referentiality, the extent to which a field cites mostly its own literature. Economics is described as historically highly self-referential, which can impede integration with external knowledge systems needed for Earth-economy synthesis.


Practical Implication for Research Design
The implication is that interdisciplinary integration is not only a technical task but a social and institutional one. Model architecture must therefore bridge differences in assumptions, data conventions, methods, and evidentiary standards.

title: Valuation
section: Component Two: Macroeconomic Architecture with GTAP and CGE
text:
Component Two: Macroeconomic Architecture with GTAP and CGE

Why GTAP Is Central in This Workflow
The second architecture component is the macroeconomic model, implemented through GTAP. GTAP is presented as a major global platform for harmonized economic and trade data and has long-standing institutional uptake across international organizations.


Two Core Assets: Database and Model
GTAP provides a structured database with broad regional and sectoral coverage across multiple base years, and it also provides a computable general equilibrium model that operationalizes those data for simulation and policy analysis.


Why CGE Rather Than Simpler Alternatives
The lecture identifies computable general equilibrium modeling as a practical sweet spot for Earth-economy linkage. It is rich enough to represent intersectoral and international propagation effects while remaining tractable for scenario analysis.


What “Computable” Means in Practice
Computable means the model can be solved numerically for large systems of linked markets and is anchored in empirical data rather than purely stylized abstraction. As model dimensionality increases, numerical feasibility becomes a central design constraint.


What “General” Means in Practice
General means economy-wide linkage rather than partial-equilibrium isolation. A policy shock in one sector or region can propagate through substitution, trade, and price channels into many other markets.


What “Equilibrium” Means in Practice
Equilibrium refers to a state in which supply and demand balance across modeled markets while household and firm behavior follows optimization assumptions. The lecture acknowledges that these assumptions are stylized, yet still useful for aggregate prediction and policy scenario comparison.


Cross-Region Shock Transmission Example
The lecture gives a concrete example: restricting palm oil expansion in Indonesia may affect substitute oils in other regions, including soybean oil markets in the United States. This illustrates why linked global structure is necessary when analyzing environmental policy in trade-connected systems.


Sectoral Resolution and Ecosystem-Service Linkage
Sectoral detail is crucial for linking ecosystem-service shocks to economic outcomes. Pollination effects, for example, cannot be represented well in a single-aggregate-crop model because crop-level pollinator dependence differs substantially.


Distributional Insight Across Countries
Country-level granularity enables analysis of winners and losers across regions, an essential feature for real policy deliberation where distributional effects shape feasibility and political acceptance.

title: Valuation
text:
Closing Position and Forward Link

Current Stopping Point in the Lecture Sequence
The lecture closes after establishing why CGE-based macroeconomic structure is a strong pairing with high-resolution Earth-system modeling. The conceptual architecture is now in place, with the first component covered in depth and the second introduced at an operational level.


Next Steps in Subsequent Sessions
Future lectures are framed as deeper technical walkthroughs with worked examples that connect model structure to concrete analytical outputs. Students are reminded to review Assignment 4 and complete submission through Canvas as the applied component of this course phase.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
Everything in this book can be understood without calculus.
This appendix exists for readers who want:

a slightly more formal lens,
a bridge to advanced modeling,
or a preview of how these ideas look in equations.

Nothing here is required for the main text.
Think of it as a translation guide between:

verbal system thinking, and

the language used inside Earth–economy models.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
Everything in this book can be understood without calculus.
This appendix exists for readers who want:

a slightly more formal lens,
a bridge to advanced modeling,
or a preview of how these ideas look in equations.

Nothing here is required for the main text.
Think of it as a translation guide between:

verbal system thinking, and

the language used inside Earth–economy models.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
2 Stocks and flows in symbols
Throughout the book we used the idea:

Next period’s stock = current stock + inflows − outflows

In symbols:
S_{t+1} = S_t + I_t − O_t
Where:

S_t is the stock at time t,
I_t is the inflow,
O_t is the outflow.

Examples:

Carbon:

C_{t+1} = C_t + Emissions_t − NaturalRemoval_t

Forest:

F_{t+1} = F_t + Growth(F_t) − Harvest_t − Conversion_t
This is the backbone of every Earth–economy model.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
3 Growth functions
A renewable resource often follows a curve like:
G(S) = r S (1 − S/K)
You do not need to memorize this.
It simply says:

small stocks grow slowly,
medium stocks grow quickly,
large stocks slow as they approach a limit K.

Graphically, this produces a “hill” shape.
The key insight is qualitative:

Regeneration is not constant.
It depends on the state of the system.

That is why thresholds and tipping points exist.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
4 Harvest and decision rules
A simple behavioral rule might be:
H_t = h · S_t
Where:

h is the harvest rate.

Then:
S_{t+1} = S_t + G(S_t) − h S_t
You can see immediately:

if h is too large,
the stock declines,
even if growth is positive.

Policy acts on h.
Institutions decide:

who sets it,
how it is enforced,
and whose interests it reflects.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
5 Prices and behavior
In economic models, behavior often takes the form:
Quantity = f(Price, Income, Technology, Rules)
For example:
EnergyUse = a − b·Price + c·Income
This is not a claim about reality.
It is a machine:

change a price,
observe how use responds,
propagate the effect through the system.

Earth–economy models connect many such machines:

production,
consumption,
land allocation,
emissions,
and ecosystem change.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
6 Inclusive wealth in symbols
In simplified form:
W = p_K K + p_H H + p_N N
Where:

K = produced capital

H = human capital

N = natural capital

p_* = shadow prices

Sustainability asks:
W_{t+1} / Population_{t+1} ≥ W_t / Population_t
This is the formal version of:

Wealth per person should not decline.

Every integrated model is, in some sense, an engine for computing W_t under different futures.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
section: 7 Why math matters—and why it is not enough
text:
7 Why math matters—and why it is not enough
Equations:

enforce consistency,
expose assumptions,
and allow simulation.

They do not:

choose values,
define justice,
or resolve conflict.

They answer:

If the world works this way, what follows?

Earth–economy modeling is not about worshiping equations.
It is about using them as:

microscopes for feedback,
stress-tests for futures,
and bridges between disciplines.

The math is a language.
The system is the story.

title: Appendix A: A Gentle Mathematical Lens
text:
8 Exercises

Translate.
Take this sentence and rewrite it in stock–flow form:
“Overfishing today reduces tomorrow’s catch.”
Interpret.
If:

C_{t+1} = C_t + E_t − R_t
explain what happens if E_t > R_t for many periods.

Reflect.
Why is it dangerous to use equations without making assumptions visible?


This appendix completes the book’s arc:

from intuition,

to systems,

to models,

to equations—

and back to judgment.

Earth–economy modeling is not about replacing thinking.
It is about giving thinking a scaffold.
This appendix gives mathematically inclined students a bridge into formal modeling without breaking the book’s accessible, systems-first ethos.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
By this point in the book, you have learned how Earth–economy models:

represent stocks and flows,
link ecosystems and economies,
explore futures through scenarios,
and evaluate policy packages.

This appendix teaches a final, essential skill:

How to read model results without surrendering judgment.

Models are powerful.
They are also fallible.
Your task is not to believe them.
Your task is to interrogate them.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
By this point in the book, you have learned how Earth–economy models:

represent stocks and flows,
link ecosystems and economies,
explore futures through scenarios,
and evaluate policy packages.

This appendix teaches a final, essential skill:

How to read model results without surrendering judgment.

Models are powerful.
They are also fallible.
Your task is not to believe them.
Your task is to interrogate them.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
2 Every model is a story
A model output is never just a number.
It is a story of the form:

If the world behaves like this,
and if people respond like that,
and if ecosystems change in these ways,
then these outcomes follow.

Every “result” rests on:

assumptions,
simplifications,
and design choices.

The question is not:

“Is this model right?”

It is:

“What world does this model assume,
and what world does it make visible?”

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
section: 3 Five questions to ask of any model
text:
3 Five questions to ask of any model

3.1 1) What is inside the system?

Which sectors are represented?
Which regions exist?
Which ecosystems appear?
Which people are visible?

Absence matters.
What is not in the model is treated as:

fixed,
irrelevant,
or exogenous.

That is a value-laden choice.



3.2 2) What are the stocks?
Ask:

What accumulates?
What depletes?
What carries memory across time?

If a system lacks:

natural capital,
social capacity,
or institutional state,

then collapse cannot occur in the model—even if it can in reality.



3.3 3) How do people behave?
Look for:

price responsiveness,
substitution rules,
technology change,
adaptation.

Are people:

perfectly informed?
infinitely flexible?
instantly adjusting?

If so, the model may:

understate disruption,
understate inequality,
and overstate smoothness.




3.4 4) Where is uncertainty?
Is uncertainty:

explored through scenarios?
confined to a few parameters?
ignored altogether?

Does the model:

allow tipping points?
allow irreversible loss?
allow surprises?

A world without uncertainty is a world without risk.



3.5 5) What is the objective?
Every model has a hidden goal:

maximize GDP,
minimize cost,
stabilize emissions,
maximize welfare,
preserve assets.

Ask:

What outcome is privileged?
What outcome is secondary?
What outcome is invisible?

This is where ethics enters.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
4 Reading a figure
Suppose you see a chart:

emissions over time,
under three scenarios.

Do not ask first:

“Which line is best?”

Ask:

What assumptions separate these lines?
What is held fixed?
What is allowed to change?
Who gains and who loses along each path?
What happens to stocks beneath the surface?

The visible curve is the surface.
The system beneath it is the content.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
5 Models as arguments
A model result is an argument.
It says:

“Given these beliefs about the world,
this policy leads here.”

Your role is not to accept or reject it.
Your role is to respond:

Are these beliefs plausible?
Are important mechanisms missing?
Does this capture what we care about?
What futures does it exclude?

Earth–economy modeling is a dialogue.
Not a verdict.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
section: 6 The Doughnut as a critique tool
text:
6 The Doughnut as a critique tool
The Doughnut gives you a powerful lens:

Does this model track social shortfall?
Does it track ecological overshoot?
Does it allow collapse?
Does it allow injustice?

A model that cannot represent:

poverty,
biodiversity loss,
or climate thresholds

cannot evaluate whether paths remain inside the safe-and-just space.
That is not a technical oversight.
It is a normative boundary.

title: Appendix C: Reading Models Critically
text:
7 Exercises

Model autopsy.
Find a policy report that uses a model.
Identify:

one assumption about behavior,

one missing stock,

one implicit objective.

Figure interrogation.
Choose a graph of projected emissions or GDP.
Write three questions that must be answered before trusting it.
Design critique.
In one paragraph, explain why “the model says so” is not an argument.


This appendix completes your training as a reader of Earth–economy models.
You now know how to:

think in systems,
design policies,
build futures,
and question the machines that claim to describe them.

That combination is rare.
And necessary.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
This book introduced a vocabulary that blends:

economics,
ecology,
systems theory,
and policy design.

Many of these words exist elsewhere—but mean something slightly different here.
This glossary is not encyclopedic.
It is operational.
Each term is defined the way it is used in Earth–economy modeling.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
This book introduced a vocabulary that blends:

economics,
ecology,
systems theory,
and policy design.

Many of these words exist elsewhere—but mean something slightly different here.
This glossary is not encyclopedic.
It is operational.
Each term is defined the way it is used in Earth–economy modeling.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
2 Core system terms
Stock
A quantity that accumulates over time and carries memory of the past.
Examples: forest area, atmospheric CO₂, soil carbon, human capital.
Flow
A change to a stock per unit time.
Examples: emissions, harvest, regeneration, investment.
Feedback
A loop in which a change in one variable alters another in a way that eventually affects the original variable.
Positive feedback amplifies change; negative feedback stabilizes.
Path / Trajectory
The sequence of system states over time. Sustainability is a property of paths, not moments.
Threshold / Tipping point
A level beyond which system behavior changes qualitatively, often irreversibly.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
3 Economic terms (reframed)
Externality
A cost or benefit of an action that falls on others and is not reflected in market prices.
Public good
A good that is non-rival and non-excludable (e.g., climate stability).
Common-pool resource
A resource that is rival but difficult to exclude others from (e.g., fisheries, groundwater).
Partial equilibrium
Analysis that isolates one market while holding others fixed.
General equilibrium
Analysis that allows all markets to adjust simultaneously.
Opportunity cost
What must be given up to obtain something else—including ecological and future losses.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
4 Sustainability terms
Natural capital
Stocks of ecosystems and biophysical systems that generate flows of value over time.
Ecosystem services
Benefits people receive from ecosystems (provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting).
Inclusive wealth
The total value of produced, human, and natural capital.
A society is sustainable if inclusive wealth per person does not decline.
Shadow price
A model-based estimate of an asset’s contribution to future well-being, even without a market price.
Robustness
Performance that remains acceptable across many uncertain futures.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
5 Modeling terms
Earth–economy model
An integrated model that represents economies as embedded in biophysical systems, tracking stocks, feedbacks, and futures.
Scenario
A conditional future: if these assumptions hold, then these outcomes follow.
Baseline
A reference scenario representing continuation of assumed trends.
Policy scenario
A scenario that introduces a specific intervention.
Counterfactual
A constructed alternative to what actually happened.
Stress test
Evaluating how a system performs under adverse or uncertain conditions.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
6 Design terms
Policy package
A coordinated set of instruments (prices, rules, investments, transfers) designed to work together.
Leakage
When an intervention reduces harm in one place but shifts it elsewhere.
Rebound
When efficiency lowers cost and increases total use.
System design
The practice of shaping rules and incentives to produce desired emergent behavior.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
7 The Doughnut lens
Social foundation
The minimum conditions for human dignity and well-being.
Ecological ceiling
The biophysical limits of Earth systems.
Safe-and-just space
The region between social shortfall and ecological overshoot.
In this book, the Doughnut is treated not as metaphor but as:

A constraint on trajectories.

Earth–economy models ask whether paths remain inside it.

title: Appendix D: A Working Glossary for Earth–Economy Thinking
text:
8 Exercises

Term translation.
Choose three terms above.
Write a sentence using each in a real policy context.
Stock hunt.
In a news article about the environment, identify:

one stock,
one flow,
one feedback.

Model reading.
Find a policy report using a “scenario.”
Rewrite one result in “if–then” form.


This glossary is not meant to be memorized.
It is meant to be used.
Every term is a handle on a system.
And every system is a future in motion.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
In 2025, Kate Raworth and co-authors published a major update to the Doughnut Economics framework in Nature — moving the Doughnut from a conceptual snapshot to a quantified, time-series dataset of global social shortfall and ecological overshoot from 2000 to 2022. :contentReferenceoaicite:0
This appendix explains what that data is, where it comes from, and how to interpret it from an Earth–economy modeling perspective — including key strengths, limitations, and how it relates to the Doughnut compass we use throughout this book.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
In 2025, Kate Raworth and co-authors published a major update to the Doughnut Economics framework in Nature — moving the Doughnut from a conceptual snapshot to a quantified, time-series dataset of global social shortfall and ecological overshoot from 2000 to 2022. :contentReferenceoaicite:0
This appendix explains what that data is, where it comes from, and how to interpret it from an Earth–economy modeling perspective — including key strengths, limitations, and how it relates to the Doughnut compass we use throughout this book.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
2 What the 2025 Doughnut analysis does

2.1 1) A quantified Doughnut over time
The 2025 paper updates the Doughnut framework by:

defining 21 dimensions of social shortfall and ecological overshoot,
using 35 quantitative indicators to measure them,
and compiling annual data from 2000–2022 wherever possible. :contentReferenceoaicite:1

This transforms the Doughnut from a static picture into a monitor of global social and ecological conditions over two decades.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
3 Data sources and construction
The analysis draws from:

the UN’s SDG Indicator Database for social outcomes,
scientific sources on planetary boundaries for ecological ceilings,
downscaled measures that try to reflect individual and country-level impacts,
and internationally comparable datasets on health, education, income, climate, biodiversity, and biochemical flows. :contentReferenceoaicite:2

Temporal coverage varies by indicator, but where possible the authors construct 30-year time series so that trends can be assessed across the early 21st century.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
4 How social shortfall is measured
“Social shortfall” is defined as:

the share of the world population missing minimum thresholds of social well-being. :contentReferenceoaicite:3

These thresholds are anchored in:

internationally recognized minimum standards (often aligned with the UN SDG targets),
criteria for what constitutes “acceptable life conditions,”
and robust, documented methods for cross-national comparison. :contentReferenceoaicite:4

Key features:

Social indicators include health, education, income security, access to basic services, and equity.
Shortfalls are measured in terms of population % below threshold, not averages — emphasizing distribution and deprivation rather than mean outcomes. :contentReferenceoaicite:5

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
5 How ecological overshoot is measured
“Ecological overshoot” refers to:

the degree to which human pressure exceeds safe levels of Earth-system processes. :contentReferenceoaicite:6

This uses the planetary boundaries framework as a ceiling for nine Earth systems (e.g., climate, biosphere integrity, biogeochemical flows). :contentReferenceoaicite:7
Key features:

Planetary boundaries define limits of safe ecological space.
Overshoot is measured as the extent to which a given indicator (e.g., CO₂ concentration or nitrogen flows) exceeds its boundary.
These ecological indicators are aggregated across systems to give a picture of total overshoot. :contentReferenceoaicite:8

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
6 Core global trends (2000–2022)

6.1 GDP growth | Social gains are modest

Global GDP more than doubled over 2000–2022.

Yet social shortfall reductions have been modest — improvements in human well-being are real but too slow to meet minimum standards for all by 2030. :contentReferenceoaicite:9

Interpretation: - This echoes the Earth–economy concern that flow metrics like GDP can mask whether asset bases (like human welfare and ecological systems) are improving. Models that focus on income alone will miss slow-moving but critical deficits.
- From a modeling lens, this suggests that inclusive wealth trajectories may diverge from GDP curves even as GDP rises. (§ Chapters 6–9)



6.2 Ecological overshoot is rising rapidly

Ecological overshoot has grown faster than social shortfall has shrunk.
By 2022, most planetary boundaries were overshot, and the rate of overshoot has increased over time. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

Interpretation: - Earth–economy models often represent dynamic stock–flow systems; the data here confirms many environmental stocks are moving outside safe ranges. - This underscores the need for policy that targets stock preservation and regeneration rather than output growth alone. (§ Chapters 2–4, 8–9)

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
7 Inequalities revealed by disaggregated data
A major contribution of the 2025 study is data disaggregation across income clusters:

Richest ~20% of countries account for >40% of ecological overshoot, despite having ~15% of the global population.

Poorest ~40% account for >60% of social shortfall, despite having ~42% of the population. :contentReferenceoaicite:11

Implication for Earth–economy modeling:

Distribution matters. Aggregate global metrics can hide underlying inequalities.
Models that treat global averages may miss key human dimensions such as capability, deprivation, and justice. (§ Chapters 4, 5, 17)

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
8 Visualization in Earth–economy models
The Nature paper illustrates:

“Doughnut rings” for 2022 showing relative shortfalls and overshoots,
Time-series “unrolled Doughnut” graphs showing trends,
Clustered Doughnuts showing distribution by income groups. :contentReferenceoaicite:12

These visuals connect directly to Earth–economy modeling practice:

They are stock diagrams with thresholds — akin to how we think about safe and just regions. (§ Chapter 2)
They show not just levels but trajectories, which is central to sustainability analysis. (§ Chapters 6–9)

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
9 Data limitations and modeling cautions
While the paper is groundbreaking, there are important caveats:

Indicators come from multiple data sources with varying quality and coverage. Comparability is imperfect. :contentReferenceoaicite:13
Planetary boundary thresholds, though scientifically grounded, are debated and evolving. :contentReferenceoaicite:14
Many social indicators require interpolation or proxy measures for missing years or countries.

From an Earth–economy modeling perspective:

Assumptions matter. How thresholds are defined and thresholds are set affects outcomes (modelling is explicit about these choices). (§ Chapter 9)
Dynamics matter. Trends are useful, but understanding why they behave this way requires integrated models that link drivers to indicators.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
section: 10 Connecting the 2025 Doughnut to Earth–Economy Modeling
text:
10 Connecting the 2025 Doughnut to Earth–Economy Modeling
The 2025 data is not merely descriptive. It provides:
✔ A monitoring baseline for evaluating model scenarios.
✔ A set of real-world indicator trajectories to calibrate and validate Earth–economy models.
✔ A demonstration of distributional patterns that models must capture to be credible.
✔ A set of thresholds that align with the Doughnut’s safe and just space constraint. (§ Chapters 9, 17)
In sum:

This dataset is one of the first large-scale quantitative bridges between earth-system limits and human well-being outcomes, enabling modeling that can test whether policies keep futures within the safe-and-just space.

title: Appendix F: Interpreting the 2025 Doughnut Economics Data
text:
11 Exercises

Indicator interpretation.
Pick one social and one ecological indicator from the 2025 Doughnut dataset.

Describe its trajectory from 2000–2022.

Explain why it would be included in an Earth–economy model.

Model calibration.
Suppose an Earth–economy model predicts a decline in ecological overshoot under a policy.
How would you use the Doughnut 2025 dataset to test the model’s validity?
Equity exploration.
Using the cluster data (richest 20% vs poorest 40%), discuss how policies could be designed to reduce both overshoot and shortfall simultaneously.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
Appendix G introduced the logic of InVEST through a few core services: water yield, pollination, and carbon.
This appendix expands that view.
It shows how InVEST operationalizes additional ecosystem services that are central to:

risk reduction,
human health,
infrastructure protection,
fisheries,
and cultural value.

Together, these models illustrate how Earth–economy systems convert:

land and seascapes → biophysical processes → services → welfare

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
Appendix G introduced the logic of InVEST through a few core services: water yield, pollination, and carbon.
This appendix expands that view.
It shows how InVEST operationalizes additional ecosystem services that are central to:

risk reduction,
human health,

and cultural value.

Together, these models illustrate how Earth–economy systems convert:

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
2 Flood risk reduction
The InVEST Flood Risk Mitigation model estimates:

how land cover alters runoff,
how water moves across terrain,
and how ecosystems reduce flood exposure.

Inputs include:

precipitation,
digital elevation models,
soil permeability,
land cover,
locations of people and assets.

Conceptually:
Runoff = f(Precipitation, Soil, Slope, LandCover) FloodRisk = Runoff × Exposure × Vulnerability
Vegetation:

increases infiltration,
slows overland flow,
reduces peak discharge.

Outputs:

maps of flood depth and extent,
avoided damage due to ecosystems,
risk metrics for downstream communities.

Earth–economy use:

evaluate upstream restoration,
price flood protection,
compare gray vs green infrastructure,
internalize disaster risk into planning.

Flood regulation turns forests and wetlands into capital assets.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
3 Sediment retention and water quality
The InVEST Sediment Delivery Ratio (SDR) and Nutrient Delivery Ratio (NDR) models estimate:

erosion from each pixel,
transport downslope,
delivery to streams,
and export to downstream waters.

Core logic:
Erosion = f(Rainfall, Soil, Slope, LandCover) Export = Erosion × Connectivity
Vegetation:

anchors soil,
traps sediment,
filters nutrients.

Outputs:

sediment and nutrient export maps,
loads by watershed,
avoided pollution due to land cover.

Earth–economy use:

link deforestation to reservoir siltation,
connect farming practices to water treatment costs,
evaluate land-based pollution policy,
quantify upstream–downstream externalities.

These services transform hillsides into infrastructure.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
4 Coastal protection
The InVEST Coastal Vulnerability model estimates:

exposure to waves and storm surge,
attenuation by reefs, mangroves, and marshes,
relative risk along coastlines.

Inputs:

bathymetry,
wave climate,
shoreline type,
habitat distribution,
sea-level rise scenarios.

Conceptually:
Exposure = f(Waves, Surge, Slope) Protection = g(HabitatType, Width, Location) Risk = Exposure − Protection
Outputs:

shoreline risk indices,
changes under habitat loss or restoration,
spatial patterns of protection.

Earth–economy use:

compare seawalls vs mangroves,
value reefs as protective assets,
integrate coastal ecosystems into adaptation plans,
couple climate risk with land-use decisions.

Here, ecosystems replace concrete.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
5 Marine fisheries and habitat
The InVEST Fisheries and Habitat Risk Assessment models estimate:

habitat quality,
exposure to stressors,
population dynamics,
and harvest outcomes.

Inputs:

habitat maps,
stressor layers (e.g., trawling, pollution),
life-history parameters,
management rules.

Conceptually:
Population_{t+1} = Population_t + Recruitment − Mortality − Harvest Recruitment = f(HabitatQuality)
Outputs:

biomass trajectories,
sustainable harvest estimates,
risk scores by habitat.

Earth–economy use:

evaluate marine protected areas,
link habitat degradation to food supply,
assess long-run wealth in fisheries,
design harvest rules that preserve stocks.

Fish become renewable capital with memory.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
6 Recreation and cultural services
The InVEST Recreation model estimates:

visitation patterns,
based on accessibility,
attractiveness,
and population proximity.

Inputs:

land cover,
protected areas,
roads and cities,
geotagged visitation data.

Outputs:

spatial patterns of recreation demand,
visitation indices,
changes under land-use scenarios.

Earth–economy use:

integrate tourism into regional planning,
value parks and green spaces,
connect urban design to well-being,
reveal non-market benefits.

This makes experience visible.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
section: 7 From service maps to system behavior
text:
7 From service maps to system behavior
Each of these models produces:

spatially explicit service supply,
under alternative land or climate scenarios.

Earth–economy models then:

translate services into productivity, risk, or welfare,
propagate changes through markets,
alter land rents and behavior,
update future land patterns.

For example:
Forest restoration → Flood risk reduction (InVEST) → Lower expected damages → Higher effective productivity → Higher land value downstream → Changed development patterns → New land-use equilibrium
This is a feedback loop.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
8 Why many services matter
A single ecosystem often provides:

carbon storage,
flood protection,
water filtration,
habitat,
recreation.

Policies that optimize one service can:

undermine others,
or produce co-benefits.

Only multi-service modeling reveals:

tradeoffs,
synergies,
and hidden costs.

Earth–economy modeling requires:

A vector of services, not a scalar.

title: Appendix H: More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
9 Exercises

Service portfolio.
Choose one landscape (coast, forest, watershed, city fringe).
List at least four ecosystem services it provides.
Tradeoff design.
Pick one service and propose a land-use change that increases it.
Identify one other service that might decline.
Coupling chain.
Write a chain linking a land policy to:

an InVEST service output,
an economic outcome,
and a long-run stock change.



InVEST shows that ecosystems are not “background.”
They are:

pipes,
buffers,
pumps,
filters,
and factories.

Earth–economy modeling is what happens
when those machines enter the economy.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
Across Appendices G–I, you have seen how InVEST represents:

production (crops, timber, fisheries),
regulation (water, floods, heat, coasts, sediment),
carbon,
habitat and biodiversity,
recreation and culture,
and energy siting.

This appendix completes the InVEST landscape by introducing models that focus on:

seasonality and water security,

groundwater and long-run hydrology,

urban access and equity,

visual and cultural value, and

coastal blue carbon systems.

These services are especially important for Earth–economy modeling because they:

operate on slow timescales,
shape human well-being directly,
and mediate climate adaptation.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
Across Appendices G–I, you have seen how InVEST represents:

production (crops, timber, fisheries),
regulation (water, floods, heat, coasts, sediment),

This appendix completes the InVEST landscape by introducing models that focus on:

These services are especially important for Earth–economy modeling because they:

operate on slow timescales,

and mediate climate adaptation.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
2 Seasonal water yield
The Seasonal Water Yield (SWY) model extends the annual water-yield logic to capture:

how water is partitioned across seasons,
how much becomes quick runoff,
and how much becomes baseflow that sustains rivers in dry periods.

Inputs:

precipitation by season,
evapotranspiration,
soils,
land cover,
topography.

Conceptually:
Quickflow = f(Rain, Imperviousness, Soil) Recharge = f(Rain, Vegetation, Soil) DrySeasonFlow ≈ AccumulatedRecharge
Outputs:

maps of baseflow contribution,
seasonal runoff,
watershed-level water security metrics.

Earth–economy use:

evaluate how deforestation alters dry-season water,
link land use to hydropower reliability,
connect watershed protection to urban water supply,
embed seasonality into economic risk.

This turns forests into intertemporal water infrastructure.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
3 Groundwater recharge and managed aquifers
Closely related, InVEST supports analysis of:

natural groundwater recharge,
and the potential for managed aquifer recharge (MAR).

These models estimate:

where infiltration occurs,
how land cover affects percolation,
and where recharge investments are most effective.

Conceptually:
Recharge = f(Soil, Slope, Vegetation, Rain) AquiferStock_{t+1} = AquiferStock_t + Recharge − Extraction
Outputs:

recharge maps,
priority zones for protection or investment,
long-run water balance implications.

Earth–economy use:

connect land policy to water scarcity,
represent aquifers as stocks,
evaluate drought resilience,
integrate water security into inclusive wealth.

Aquifers become hidden capital accounts.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
4 Urban nature access
The Urban Nature Access model estimates:

how easily people can reach green space,
given distance, barriers, and population density,
and how access changes under development scenarios.

Inputs:

green space maps,
street networks,
population distribution,
travel thresholds.

Conceptually:
Access = f(Distance, Connectivity, Population)
Outputs:

maps of population served by green space,
equity metrics by neighborhood,
changes under land-use plans.

Earth–economy use:

connect urban form to well-being,
evaluate green infrastructure equity,
treat access as a social stock,
link planning to health outcomes.

This model makes who benefits spatially explicit.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
5 Scenic quality
The Scenic Quality model estimates:

how visually intrusive features (roads, mines, towers) affect landscapes,
who sees them,
and how far their visual influence extends.

Inputs:

digital elevation models,
land cover,
locations of visual disturbances,
viewer locations.

Conceptually:
VisualImpact = f(Visibility, Distance, Contrast) ScenicQuality = Baseline − VisualImpact
Outputs:

maps of visual degradation,
counts of people affected,
scenario comparisons.

Earth–economy use:

integrate aesthetics into land planning,
evaluate infrastructure siting,
connect landscape change to tourism and identity,
formalize cultural services.

This turns “sense of place” into a system variable.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
6 Coastal blue carbon
The Coastal Blue Carbon model estimates:

carbon stored in mangroves, marshes, and seagrass,
emissions from degradation,
sequestration from restoration.

Inputs:

habitat maps,
carbon pool parameters,
transition scenarios.

Conceptually:
C_total = C_biomass + C_soil ΔC = C_future − C_current
Outputs:

coastal carbon stocks,
avoided emissions,
mitigation potential.

Earth–economy use:

integrate coastal ecosystems into climate policy,
value restoration as mitigation,
link sea-level rise to asset loss,
treat wetlands as climate capital.

Here, shorelines become carbon infrastructure.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
7 Why these services matter
These models share three properties that are central to Earth–economy thinking:

They are stock-based.

Aquifers, baseflow, access, scenic quality, blue carbon
all accumulate or erode over time.

They are spatially unequal.

Benefits and losses fall on specific communities.

They mediate resilience.

Drought survival, heat stress, flood recovery, identity.


They therefore connect directly to:

inclusive wealth,
intergenerational equity,
and robustness under uncertainty.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
section: 8 From hidden services to explicit systems
text:
8 From hidden services to explicit systems
Consider this chain:
Urban expansion → Loss of wetlands and trees → ↓ Blue carbon, ↓ cooling, ↓ recharge → ↑ Heat exposure, ↑ flood risk, ↓ water security → ↑ Health costs, ↓ productivity → Changed wages, rents, and migration → New land-use equilibrium
Without InVEST-style services, this chain is invisible.
With them, it becomes:

computable,
testable,
and designable.

title: Appendix J: Still More Ecosystem Services with InVEST
text:
9 Exercises

Equity lens.
Choose one of the services in this appendix.
Describe how it could widen or narrow inequality across neighborhoods.
Stock mapping.
For seasonal water yield or groundwater, identify:

the stock,
the inflows,
the outflows,
one policy lever.

Coupled future.
Sketch how coastal blue carbon could be integrated into:

a national climate plan,
and an Earth–economy model.



With Appendices G–J, InVEST appears not as a toolkit of niche models,
but as a catalog of ecological production functions.
Earth–economy modeling is what happens
when every one of those functions
is allowed to reshape the economy.
